claim: Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ animals were born alive and cannot be distinguished from their wild-type littermates by their outer appearance or activity at birth.
source: Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ animals were born alive and cannot be distinguished from their wild-type littermates by their outer appearance or activity at birth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: At postnatal day 2, Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice can be identified by their slightly diminished body size.
source: However, at postnatal day 2, Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice can be identified by their slightly diminished body size.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: The reduced size and activity in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mutants became more pronounced as postnatal development proceeded.
source: The reduced size and activity in these mutants became more pronounced as postnatal development proceeded.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Mortality was observed in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice at various time points postnatally, especially between postnatal day 3 and 7 (mostly after day 4/5).
source: Mortality was observed in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice at various time points postnatally, especially between postnatal day 3 and 7 (mostly after day 4/5).
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: A small number of Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice survived beyond postnatal day 7.
source: Interestingly, a small number of Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice survived beyond postnatal day 7.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Vangl2-deficient lungs consisted of enlarged saccules and failed to generate alveoli.
source: Vangl2-deficient lungs consisted of enlarged saccules (Figure 1A) and failed to generate alveoli (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Vangl2 is essential for alveolar formation during lung development.
source: These results establish an essential role of Vangl2 in alveolar formation (traditionally defined as P5-25 in mice) during lung development.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Loss of Vangl2 mediated by Sox9-Cre does not disrupt branching morphogenesis or saccule formation.
source: Loss of Vangl2 mediated by Sox9-Cre thus does not disrupt branching morphogenesis or saccule formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: At postnatal day 3, enlarged saccules were discerned in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs in comparison with controls.
source: At postnatal day 3, enlarged saccules were discerned in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs in comparison with controls under a dissecting microscope (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy of control and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs revealed lack of rudimentary secondary septa in the mutant lungs.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of control and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs revealed lack of rudimentary secondary septa (arrows) in the mutant lungs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No apparent defects in other organs were found in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
source: No apparent defects in other organs were found in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The primary septa in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs underwent a similar thinning process in the first three days of postnatal life.
source: The primary septa in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs underwent a similar thinning process in the first three days of postnatal life.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: The primary septa in mutant lungs failed to engender subsequent modification and retained a relatively thin appearance.
source: However, the primary septa in mutant lungs failed to engender subsequent modification and retained a relatively thin appearance (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of PCP signaling in the distal lung cells has a profound influence on the normal progression and development of the primary septa to generate secondary septa.
source: These results suggest that loss of PCP signaling in the distal lung cells has a profound influence on the normal progression and development of the primary septa to generate secondary septa.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Only a very small number of primordial secondary septa could be detected in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Only a very small number of primordial secondary septa could be detected in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Vangl2-deficient lungs contained enlarged saccules with an increased mean linear intercept (MLI).
source: As a result, Vangl2-deficient lungs contained enlarged saccules (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 7) with an increased mean linear intercept (MLI, a measure of air space size) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and MLI measurements shown in Figure 1B, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Disruption of secondary septa formation in the absence of PCP signaling in the distal lung epithelium likely led to respiratory failure and neonatal lethality.
source: Disruption of secondary septa formation in the absence of PCP signaling in the distal lung epithelium likely led to respiratory failure and neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Vangl2f/f; Dermo1Cre/+ and Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice displayed lung phenotypes resembling those in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
source: We found that Vangl2f/f; Dermo1Cre/+ and Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice displayed lung phenotypes (Figure 1E, F, G, H and I) resembling those in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E, F, G, H, and I.

claim: Secondary septa failed to form in Vangl2f/f; Dermo1Cre/+ or Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice.
source: Secondary septa failed to form in Vangl2f/f; Dermo1Cre/+ or Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice, saccules were enlarged with an increased mean linear intercept, and many of the mutants failed to survive beyond postnatal day 7 (Figure 1E, F, G, H and I).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E, F, G, H, and I.

claim: PCP signaling operates in both the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and each process is essential for secondary septa formation by controlling distinct aspects of alveologenesis.
source: We conclude that PCP signaling operates in both the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and each process is essential for secondary septa formation by controlling distinct aspects of alveologenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice in different compartments.

claim: Ror2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice displayed neonatal lethality and their lungs failed to produce secondary septa.
source: Indeed, Ror2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice displayed neonatal lethality and their lungs failed to produce secondary septa (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Lung phenotypes between Ror2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice are similar.
source: A detailed phenotypic analysis (Figure 2A and B) confirmed the similarity of lung phenotypes between Ror2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Ror2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice died postnatally due to alveolar defects, resembling phenotypes observed in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice.
source: As predicted by our model of a Ror2–Vangl2 cascade, these mice died postnatally due to alveolar defects (Figure 2C and D), resembling phenotypes observed in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Ror2 plays a key role in activating Vangl2 in either alveolar epithelial cells or mesenchymal myofibroblasts.
source: Taken together, these studies established a key role of Ror2 in activating Vangl2 in either alveolar epithelial cells or mesenchymal myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Ror2-deficient mice.

claim: Treatment of neonatal mice with Wnt-C59 or LGK974, inhibitors of PORCUPINE, resulted in alveolar defects.
source: Consistent with the involvement of Wnt signaling in alveolar development, treatment of neonatal mice with Wnt-C59 (Proffitt et al., 2013) or LGK974 (WNT-974) (Liu et al., 2013), inhibitors of PORCUPINE, resulted in alveolar defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of Porcn in the lung mesenchyme by creating Porcnf/f; Dermo1Cre/+ mice or in lung myofibroblasts by generating Porcnf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice led to alveolar defects.
source: Moreover, inactivation of Porcn in the lung mesenchyme by creating Porcnf/f; Dermo1Cre/+ mice or in lung myofibroblasts by generating Porcnf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice also led to alveolar defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2E.

claim: Wnt signals in the lung mesenchyme initiate PCP signaling for alveolar development.
source: These results support the notion that Wnt signals in the lung mesenchyme initiate PCP signaling for alveolar development.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Porcn-deficient mice.

claim: Wnt5a mRNA was mainly expressed in myofibroblasts and barely any signal was detected in the lung epithelium.
source: We found that Wnt5a mRNA was mainly expressed in myofibroblasts and barely any signal was detected in the lung epithelium (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by PLISH data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ mice were born alive but many displayed a smaller body size at postnatal day 4 or 5.
source: Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ mice were born alive but many displayed a smaller body size at postnatal day 4 or 5.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Phenotypic analysis of Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ lungs revealed defective alveolar formation.
source: Phenotypic analysis of Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ lungs revealed defective alveolar formation (Figure 2F) albeit the alveolar defects were not as pervasive as those caused by loss of Ror2 or Vangl2.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis controls alveolar formation.
source: Taken together, our genetic studies have established a Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis in controlling alveolar formation (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Wnt5a, Ror2, and Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Mesenchymal Wnt5a triggers a Ror2/Vangl2–mediated cascade in both lung epithelium and mesenchyme.
source: In this process, mesenchymal Wnt5a triggers a Ror2/Vangl2–mediated cascade in both lung epithelium and mesenchyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Wnt5a, Ror2, and Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: No apparent asymmetric localization of VANGL2 was found in alveolar type I cells, alveolar type II cells or myofibroblasts.
source: To our surprise, we found no apparent asymmetric localization of VANGL2 in alveolar type I cells, alveolar type II cells or myofibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis controls cellular properties of individual lung cells regardless of asymmetric activation of PCP components.
source: This led to our new model in which a Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis controls cellular properties of individual lung cells regardless of asymmetric activation of PCP components.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of asymmetric VANGL2 localization.

claim: Interstitial fibroblasts that expressed PDGFRA failed to proliferate as revealed by reduced EdU incorporation in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraH2BGFP/+; Sox9Cre/+ mice in comparison with PdgfraH2BGFP/+ mice (controls).
source: Indeed, we found that interstitial fibroblasts that expressed PDGFRA failed to proliferate as revealed by reduced EdU incorporation in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraH2BGFP/+; Sox9Cre/+ mice in comparison with PdgfraH2BGFP/+ mice (controls) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myofibroblasts (SMA+) in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs failed to migrate to the prospective sites of secondary septa formation.
source: Moreover, myofibroblasts (SMA+) in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs failed to migrate to the prospective sites of secondary septa formation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Decreased myofibroblast proliferation first appeared at postnatal day 2 when PDGFRA+ interstitial fibroblasts started to express SMA and became myofibroblasts.
source: Decreased myofibroblast proliferation first appeared at postnatal day 2 when PDGFRA+ interstitial fibroblasts started to express SMA and became myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: By postnatal day 3, the number of PDGFRA+ interstitial fibroblasts had vastly decreased in the mutant lungs.
source: By postnatal day 3, the number of PDGFRA+ interstitial fibroblasts had vastly decreased in the mutant lungs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both SMA and elastin production was significantly curtailed in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: As expected, both SMA and elastin production was significantly curtailed in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PDGFA is produced primarily in alveolar type I and type II cells and signals to Pdgfra-expressing fibroblasts/myofibroblasts to regulate their proliferation and migration.
source: PDGFA is produced primarily in alveolar type I and type II cells and signals to Pdgfra-expressing fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (Chen and Krasnow, 2012; Gouveia et al., 2017) to regulate their proliferation and migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No difference in PDGFA ligand production was found between control and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by both qPCR analysis and in situ hybridization.
source: While loss of either Pdgfa (Boström et al., 1996; Lindahl et al., 1997) or Pdgfra (Sun et al., 2000) can result in loss of secondary septa (Noskovičová et al., 2015), we found no difference in PDGFA ligand production between control and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by both qPCR analysis and in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and in situ hybridization data, and citations to previous studies.

claim: PDGFA was expressed more frequently in AT1 cells than AT2 cells and PDGFA expression levels were higher in AT1 cells than AT2 cells.
source: We found that PDGFA was expressed more frequently in AT1 cells than AT2 cells and PDGFA expression levels were higher in AT1 cells than AT2 cells (Figure 3E), consistent with single-cell RNA-Seq data (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figure 3E and citation to previous single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: PDGFA displayed a similar pattern and intensity between control and Vangl2-deficient lungs.
source: PDGFA displayed a similar pattern and intensity between control and Vangl2-deficient lungs (Figure 3F), consistent with no reduction in Pdgfa transcript levels in the absence of Vangl2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by LacZ staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The levels of PDGFRA in a single myofibroblast were unaffected in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Consistent with our model, while the levels of PDGFRA in a single myofibroblast were unaffected (Figure 3G), phosphorylation of PDGFRA in individual myofibroblasts upon PDGFA ligand binding was significantly reduced in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA in individual myofibroblasts upon PDGFA ligand binding was significantly reduced in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Consistent with our model, while the levels of PDGFRA in a single myofibroblast were unaffected (Figure 3G), phosphorylation of PDGFRA in individual myofibroblasts upon PDGFA ligand binding was significantly reduced in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of the downstream kinases, such as AKT, was drastically diminished in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs in comparison with controls.
source: In addition, activation of the downstream kinases, such as AKT (a serine-threonine kinase) (Demoulin and Essaghir, 2014), was drastically diminished in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs in comparison with controls by immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and citation to previous studies.

claim: PDGFA-3xFLAG in the media incubated with Vangl1/2-deficient cells was significantly reduced.
source: Using this assay, we determined the amount of PDGFA-3xFLAG released from control and Vangl1/2-deficient cells. PDGFA-3xFLAG in the media incubated with Vangl1/2-deficient cells was significantly reduced (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The intracellular levels of PDGFA-GFP were increased in Vangl1/2-deficient cells.
source: Indeed, we found that the intracellular levels of PDGFA-GFP were increased in Vangl1/2-deficient cells (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inactivation of Vangl1/2 in alveolar type II cells led to alveolar defects.
source: Consistent with our model in which the PDGF ligand fails to be released from alveolar epithelial cells in the absence of Vangl1/2, inactivation of Vangl1/2 in alveolar type II cells (Surfactant protein C [SP-C or SPC]+ encoded by Sftpc) led to alveolar defects. We generated Vangl1gt/gt; Vangl2f/f; SftpcCreER/+ mice and administered tamoxifen to these animals at P2. Activation of CreER by tamoxifen in SPC+ cells (Lin et al., 2012) induced Vangl2 removal. Analysis of lungs at P10 revealed areas of defective alveolar development that was associated with loss of Vangl1/2 (Figure 3K, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and citation to previous studies.

claim: The structure of the Golgi apparatus was altered in Vangl1/2-deficient cells.
source: We also discovered that the structure of the Golgi apparatus was altered in Vangl1/2-deficient cells. Compared to control cells in which the Golgi apparatus was properly polarized inside the cells, the Golgi stacks were dispersed in Vangl1/2-deficient cells (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Alveolar type II cells make direct cell-cell contacts with myofibroblasts via cellular processes that pass through the basement membrane.
source: Alveolar type II cells make direct cell-cell contacts with myofibroblasts via cellular processes that pass through the basement membrane (Figure 3M; Brody et al., 1982; Adamson and King, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3M and citations to previous studies.

claim: TEM studies revealed loss of cellular processes from alveolar type II cells in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs, which were no longer in direct contact with myofibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, TEM studies revealed loss of cellular processes from alveolar type II cells in Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs, which were no longer in direct contact with myofibroblasts (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Alveolar type I and type II cells utilize a Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 cascade to control PDGF ligand trafficking and release and contribute to secondary septa formation.
source: Taken together, our studies support a model in which alveolar type I and type II cells utilize a Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 cascade to control PDGF ligand trafficking and release and contribute to secondary septa formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA in individual myofibroblasts upon PDGFA ligand binding was reduced in Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ lungs.
source: We found that phosphorylation of PDGFRA in individual myofibroblasts upon PDGFA ligand binding was reduced in Wnt5af/f; Tbx4Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), while the levels of PDGFRA were unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Elimination of mesenchymal Wnt signaling prior to alveologenesis in Porcnf/f; Dermo1Cre/+ lungs led to reduced PDGF signal transduction without affecting PDGF ligand production or differentiation of alveolar type I and type II cells.
source: Moreover, elimination of mesenchymal Wnt signaling (including WNT5A secretion from fibroblasts) prior to alveologenesis in Porcnf/f; Dermo1Cre/+ lungs led to reduced PDGF signal transduction without affecting PDGF ligand production or differentiation of alveolar type I and type II cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Loss of PDGF ligand resulted in depletion of WNT5A-producing fibroblasts/myofibroblasts and a reduction in Wnt5a transcript levels.
source: Conversely, loss of PDGF ligand resulted in depletion of WNT5A-producing fibroblasts/myofibroblasts and a reduction in Wnt5a transcript levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: A positive feedback loop between WNT5A and PDGFA generates an adequate number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts required for alveologenesis.
source: These results support a positive feedback loop between WNT5A and PDGFA to generate an adequate number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts required for alveologenesis (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Wnt5a and Pdgfa-deficient mice.

claim: Loss of Vangl2 and Ror2 showed similar changes in many pathways.
source: We also performed RNA-Seq analysis on control and Ror2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs collected at P2 and P5 (Figure 4C and D). We expect that many changes in transcriptional responses would follow a similar trend in lungs deficient in epithelial Vangl2 or Ror2, if Ror2 is responsible for mediating Vangl2 activity. Indeed, loss of Vangl2 and Ror2 showed similar changes in many pathways, affirming the genetic studies in which they function in the same axis.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Myofibroblast proliferation was diminished in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs but only at later stages of postnatal development while the initial expansion of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was unaffected.
source: We found that myofibroblast proliferation was also diminished in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs but only at later stages of postnatal development while the initial expansion of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was unaffected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both SMA and elastin production was significantly reduced in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs.
source: Both SMA and elastin production was significantly reduced in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Phalloidin staining of F-actin revealed a disorganized actomyosin cytoskeleton and smooth muscle actin failed to produce organized stress fibers in mutant myofibroblasts.
source: Phalloidin staining of F-actin (filamentous) revealed a disorganized actomyosin cytoskeleton and smooth muscle actin failed to produce organized stress fibers in mutant myofibroblasts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At P5 while PDGFRA+/SMA+ myofibroblasts had migrated to the prospective sites of secondary septa in control lungs, PDGFRA+/SMA+ cells in the mutant lungs stayed in the primary septa.
source: We also analyzed fibroblast/myofibroblast distribution in Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs at P0 and P5 (Figure 5D). We found no difference in the distribution of PDGFRA+ fibroblasts at P0. However, at P5 while PDGFRA+/SMA+ myofibroblasts had migrated to the prospective sites of secondary septa in control lungs, PDGFRA+/SMA+ cells in the mutant lungs stayed in the primary septa.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: While control myofibroblasts occupied the cell-free area after 36–48 hr, only scant Vangl2-deficient myofibroblasts were detected in the cell-free area during this time period.
source: To test this idea, we isolated myofibroblasts from control and Vangl2f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs and seeded them onto the migration chamber. The rate of myofibroblast migration into the cell-free area was measured. While control myofibroblasts occupied the cell-free area after 36–48 hr, only scant Vangl2-deficient myofibroblasts were detected in the cell-free area during this time period (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by wound recovery assay data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The mobility of myofibroblasts was compromised due to loss of PCP signaling in these cells.
source: This indicates that the mobility of myofibroblasts was compromised due to loss of PCP signaling in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the wound recovery assay data.

claim: Phosphorylated Cofilin and LIM-kinase (LIMK) were significantly increased in Vangl2-deficient alveolar type I cells, compared to controls.
source: We then searched for other markers for the actomyosin cytoskeleton and found that phosphorylated Cofilin and LIM-kinase (LIMK) were significantly increased in Vangl2-deficient alveolar type I cells, compared to controls (Figure 6A, B and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A, B, and D.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cofilin by LIMK inhibited its ability to depolymerize actin, leading to a failure in actin bundle remodeling.
source: Phosphorylation of Cofilin by LIMK inhibited its ability to depolymerize actin, leading to a failure in actin bundle remodeling (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Cofilin and LIMK function.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed slender Vangl2-deficient AT1 cells that failed to fold up to encase myofibroblasts.
source: Disruption of the actomyosin cytoskeleton in alveolar type I cells in the absence of PCP signaling raised the possibility that AT1 cells failed to undergo morphogenetic adjustment to sheathe myofibroblasts and capillaries during secondary septa formation. Indeed, immunohistochemical analysis revealed slender Vangl2-deficient AT1 cells that failed to fold up to encase myofibroblasts (Figure 6C and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C and E.

claim: AT1 cells in control lungs at P3 displayed folding to sheathe myofibroblasts that had migrated to the prospective sites of secondary septa formation.
source: This observation was further validated by TEM studies of control and Vangl2f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs. For instance, AT1 cells in control lungs at P3 displayed folding to sheathe myofibroblasts that had migrated to the prospective sites of secondary septa formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Such coordinated morphological changes in AT1 cells did not occur in the mutant lungs.
source: By contrast, such coordinated morphological changes in AT1 cells did not occur in the mutant lungs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PCP signaling operates in both the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and control distinct aspects of cellular properties in each compartment necessary for alveologenesis.
source: Taken together, we conclude that PCP signaling operates in both the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and control distinct aspects of cellular properties in each compartment necessary for alveologenesis. This includes ligand secretion, cell shape change and migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice in different compartments.

claim: Although a similar number of alveolospheres was obtained, the size distribution of the alveolospheres derived from Vangl1/2-deficient AT1 cells was dominated by those with a smaller size.
source: In the absence of Vangl1/2, differentiation of AT2 cells and proliferation of AT2 and AT1 cells were unaffected. However, although a similar number of alveolospheres was obtained, the size distribution of the alveolospheres derived from Vangl1/2-deficient AT1 cells was dominated by those with a smaller size (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Analysis of lungs at P7 revealed areas of defective alveolar development due to loss of Vangl1/2 in AT1 cells.
source: To assess the role of AT1 cells in alveologenesis, we generated Vangl1gt/gt; Vangl2f/f; Aqp5CreER/+ mice and administered tamoxifen to these animals at P2. Activation of CreER by tamoxifen in Aquaporin 5 (AQP5)+ cells induced Vangl2 removal in AT1 cells. Analysis of lungs at P7 revealed areas of defective alveolar development due to loss of Vangl1/2 (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: After 4 weeks post-bleomycin administration, lung repair was extensive in control lungs and newly formed alveoli had replaced the damaged lung tissues.
source: We then subjected these animals to bleomycin following the standard protocol. After 4 weeks post-bleomycin administration, lung repair was extensive in control lungs and newly formed alveoli had replaced the damaged lung tissues (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6J and K.

claim: Fewer GFP+ alveoli in Vangl1gt/gt; Vangl2f/f; SftpcCreER/+; ROSA26mTmG/+ mice were found and they failed to reach the same size as that in control lungs.
source: By contrast, fewer GFP+ alveoli in Vangl1gt/gt; Vangl2f/f; SftpcCreER/+; ROSA26mTmG/+ mice were found and they failed to reach the same size as that in control lungs (Figure 6J and K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6J and K, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vangl1/2-deficient AT1 cells were compromised in their ability to form new alveoli.
source: This suggests that Vangl1/2-deficient AT1 cells were compromised in their ability to form new alveoli although Vangl1/2-deficient AT2 cells could also contribute to the observed defects in alveolar repair.
evidence: This is inferred from the bleomycin-induced alveolar repair assay data.

claim: The expression levels of WNT5A and VANGL2 were reduced in COPD/emphysema patients.
source: To explore whether studies of PCP signaling in alveolar formation in mice recapitulate human diseases, we assessed PCP signaling in lung tissues of COPD/emphysema patients (Figure 7A and B). We found that the expression levels of WNT5A and VANGL2 were reduced (Figure 7C), suggesting a link between PCP signaling and alveolar loss/regeneration in these patients.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: SERPINA3, SAA3 and CD14, whose expression was increased in Vangl2-deficient murine lungs, are activated in COPD patients and are biomarkers for COPD.
source: It is interesting to note that SERPINA3 (a protease inhibitor), SAA3 (serum amyloid A) and CD14, whose expression was increased in Vangl2-deficient murine lungs (Figure 4E), are activated in COPD patients and are biomarkers for COPD (Bozinovski et al., 2008; Wood et al., 2009; von Scheele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous studies.

claim: The PCP pathway controls PDGF signaling from alveolar type I and II cells to fibroblasts/myofibroblasts to promote their proliferation.
source: Through genetic and molecular approaches, we decipher PCP signaling through a Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis as a key element in mediating cell-cell interactions between alveolar cells (type I and type II) and myofibroblasts. The PCP pathway controls PDGF signaling from alveolar type I and II cells to fibroblasts/myofibroblasts to promote their proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: A positive feedback loop between WNT5A and PDGF facilitates expansion of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts.
source: A positive feedback loop between WNT5A and PDGF facilitates expansion of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Wnt5a and Pdgfa-deficient mice.

claim: Orchestrated movement between alveolar type I cells and myofibroblasts is regulated by PCP signaling, including cell shape change of alveolar type I cells and migration of myofibroblasts.
source: Subsequently, orchestrated movement between alveolar type I cells and myofibroblasts is regulated by PCP signaling, including cell shape change of alveolar type I cells and migration of myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: These critical events require changes in cellular properties mediated by PCP signaling and reflect a novel facet of PCP function.
source: These critical events require changes in cellular properties mediated by PCP signaling and reflect a novel facet of PCP function.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: The primary function of the Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis is to modulate the cellular properties of lung cells required for alveolar formation.
source: Surprisingly, these processes do not appear to involve the classical tissue polarity, in which asymmetric distribution of PCP components is associated with polarization of cells (Ossipova et al., 2015). Instead, the primary function of the Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis is to modulate the cellular properties of lung cells required for alveolar formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of asymmetric VANGL2 localization and citation to previous studies.

claim: PCP signaling exerts its effects at the subcellular levels via controlling the cytoskeleton in alveolar type I, type II cells and myofibroblasts.
source: Our work shows that PCP signaling exerts its effects at the subcellular levels via controlling the cytoskeleton in alveolar type I, type II cells and myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Loss of Ror2 in either lung epithelium or mesenchyme recapitulates phenotypes due to lack of Vangl2.
source: Loss of Ror2 in either lung epithelium or mesenchyme recapitulates phenotypes due to lack of Vangl2. This supports a crucial role of ROR2 in activating VANGL2 and downstream events.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Ror2-deficient mice.

claim: Morphological changes of AT1 cells induced by PCP signaling are required for secondary septa elongation.
source: Our genetic and molecular studies support a new model in which morphological changes of AT1 cells induced by PCP signaling are required for secondary septa elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: Secondary septa development relies on coordinated cell shape changes in both alveolar epithelial cells and myofibroblasts.
source: Thus, secondary septa development relies on coordinated cell shape changes in both alveolar epithelial cells and myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: A key element in secondary septa development is an altered actomyosin cytoskeleton controlled by the Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis.
source: A key element in this process is an altered actomyosin cytoskeleton controlled by the Wnt5a–Ror2–Vangl2 axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: PDGF ligands produced in alveolar cells fail to signal to myofibroblasts in Vangl2-deficient lungs.
source: Our analysis of Vangl2-deficient lungs revealed that PDGF ligands produced in alveolar cells fail to signal to myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic analysis of Vangl2-deficient mice.

claim: PDGF signal reception is compromised by loss of cell-cell contacts between alveolar cells and mesenchymal myofibroblasts.
source: We propose that PDGF signal reception is compromised by loss of cell-cell contacts between alveolar cells and mesenchymal myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.
